'''David Alan Leigh''' (born 31 May 1963)<ref name=whoswho/> [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] [[FRSE]] [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry|FRSC]] is a British [[chemist]], [[Royal Society]] Research Professor<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2016/09/leading-scientists-awarded-royal-society-research-professorships/|title=Leading scientists awarded Royal Society Research Professorships &#124; Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref> and, since 2014, the [[Sir Samuel Hall Chair of Chemistry]] in the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Manchester|Department of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Manchester]]. He was previously the Forbes Chair of Organic Chemistry at the [[University of Edinburgh]] (2001–2012) and Professor of Synthetic Chemistry at the [[University of Warwick]] (1998–2001).<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kay | first1 = E. R. | last2 = Leigh | first2 = D. A. | authorlink2  = David Leigh (scientist)| last3 = Zerbetto | first3 = F. | title = Synthetic Molecular Motors and Mechanical Machines | doi = 10.1002/anie.200504313 | pmid = 17133632 | journal = Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume = 46 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 72–191 | year = 2007 | bibcode = 2007ACIE...46...72K }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Brouwer | first1 = A. M. | last2 = Frochot | first2 = C. | last3 = Gatti | first3 = F. G. | last4 = Leigh | first4 = D. A.| authorlink4 = David Leigh (scientist) | last5 = Mottier | first5 = L. | last6 = Paolucci | first6 = F. | last7 = Roffia | first7 = S. | last8 = Wurpel | first8 = G. W. | doi = 10.1126/science.1057886 | title = Photoinduction of Fast, Reversible Translational Motion in a Hydrogen-Bonded Molecular Shuttle | journal = Science | volume = 291 | issue = 5511 | pages = 2124–2128 | year = 2001 | pmid =  11251112| bibcode = 2001Sci...291.2124B | s2cid = 31639520 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He is President-elect of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (2026–28; President 2028–2030).<ref>[https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/david-leigh-wins-vote-to-become-next-president-elect-of-the-royal-society-of-chemistry/4023622.article David Leigh wins vote to become next president-elect of the Royal Society of Chemistry], rsc.org, 2 June 2026.</ref>

==Education==
Leigh was educated at [[Codsall Community High School]] and the [[University of Sheffield]].<ref name=whoswho/>

==Career and research==
He is noted for the invention of fundamental methods to control molecular-level dynamics and entanglement. His group's experimental designs established [[Brownian ratchet]] mechanisms as a general principle for achieving directionality, transport, energy transduction and function in chemical systems far from equilibrium. Key advances include catalysis-driven (autonomous) chemically fueled systems, molecular assembly, entanglement and weaving, novel and general strategies to [[rotaxane]]s, [[catenane]]s and [[molecular knots]], and some of the earliest synthetic molecular motors, molecular robots and functional nanomachines.

Using [[mechanically-interlocked molecular architectures]] he prepared a novel molecular information ratchet<ref name=ratchet>{{Cite web|url=http://www.catenane.net/home/maxwellpaper1.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080820025210/http://www.catenane.net/home/maxwellpaper1.htm |url-status=dead |title=Leigh's Group's illustrated explanation of the "ratchet"|archivedate=20 August 2008}}</ref> that employs a mechanism reminiscent of [[Maxwell's demon]] (although it requires an energy input and so does not challenge the [[second law of thermodynamics]]).<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/technology/6320781.stm|title=Tiny engine boosts nanotech hopes|date=1 February 2007|publisher=BBC News}}</ref> He has developed a rotaxane based photoactive [[molecular switch]] with the capability of changing the hydrophobicity of a surface and thus causing small droplets of liquid to move up hill, against the force of gravity.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/4192776.stm|title=Nanotech team move water droplets|date=29 August 2005|publisher=BBC News}}</ref> In 2009 he reported the first small-molecule walker-track system in which a 'walker' can be transported directionally along a short molecular track in a manner reminiscent of the way that biological motor proteins 'walk' along biopolymers in the cell.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/News/2009/December/21120901.asp |title='Two-legged' molecular walker takes a stroll|website=Chemistry World|date= 21 December 2009}}</ref> In 2011 his research group described the smallest molecular knot prepared to date (a 76-atom-loop [[trefoil knot]] – three crossing points<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Barran | first1 = P. E. | last2 = Cole | first2 = H. L. | last3 = Goldup | first3 = S. M. | last4 = Leigh | first4 = D. A. | authorlink4 = David Leigh (scientist)| last5 = McGonigal | first5 = P. R. | last6 = Symes | first6 = M. D. | last7 = Wu | first7 = J. | last8 = Zengerle | first8 = M. | doi = 10.1002/anie.201105012 | pmid = 21919173 | title = Active-Metal Template Synthesis of a Molecular Trefoil Knot | journal = Angewandte Chemie International Edition | volume = 50 | issue = 51 | pages = 12280–12284 | year = 2011 | bibcode = 2011ACIE...5012280B | url = https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/output/1431765 }}</ref>) and also a 160-atom-loop [[pentafoil knot]] (five crossing points).<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Ayme | first1 = J. F. | last2 = Beves | first2 = J. E. | last3 = Leigh | first3 = D. A. | authorlink3 = David Leigh (scientist)| last4 = McBurney | first4 = R. T. | last5 = Rissanen | first5 = K. | last6 = Schultz | first6 = D. | doi = 10.1038/nchem.1193 | title = A synthetic molecular pentafoil knot | journal = Nature Chemistry | volume = 4 | issue = 1 | pages = 15–20 | year = 2011 | pmid =  22169866}}</ref> The Leigh group have also reported the synthesis of an 8<sub>19</sub> knot, the most complex [[molecular knot]] made to date,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Danon|first1=Jonathan J.|last2=Krüger|first2=Anneke|last3=Leigh|first3=David A.|last4=Lemonnier|first4=Jean-François|last5=Stephens|first5=Alexander J.|last6=Vitorica-Yrezabal|first6=Iñigo J.|last7=Woltering|first7=Steffen L.|year=2017|title=Braiding a molecular knot with eight crossings|journal=Science|language=en|volume=355|issue=6321|pages=159–162|doi=10.1126/science.aal1619|issn=0036-8075|pmid=28082585|bibcode=2017Sci...355..159D|s2cid=206654419|url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/braiding-a-molecular-knot-with-eight-crossings(678fc632-5cef-4f03-a6b4-cd2c719f5763).html}}</ref> and a molecular endless knot<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leigh |first1=David A. |last2=Danon |first2=Jonathan J. |last3=Fielden |first3=Stephen D. P. |last4=Lemonnier |first4=Jean-François |last5=Whitehead |first5=George F. S. |last6=Woltering |first6=Steffen L. |title=A molecular endless (7 4 ) knot |journal=Nature Chemistry |date=14 December 2020 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=117–122 |doi=10.1038/s41557-020-00594-x |pmid=33318672 |s2cid=229163544 |url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/a-molecular-endless-74-knot(5d897ba5-5995-4a00-bd4d-8c991a650e64).html }}</ref> (the smallest [[Chinese knot]]). In 2013 the Leigh group reported<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-20987065|title=Tiny molecular machine apes cellular production line|publisher=BBC News |date=11 January 2013}}</ref> a small-molecule machine capable of detaching and assembling a series of amino acid building blocks from a track into a peptide of specific sequence, a very primitive version of the task performed by the [[ribosome]]. They also invented the first autonomous chemically-fuelled [[synthetic molecular motor]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Miriam R. |last2=Solà |first2=Jordi |last3=Carlone |first3=Armando |last4=Goldup |first4=Stephen M. |last5=Lebrasseur |first5=Nathalie |last6=Leigh |first6=David A. |title=An autonomous chemically fuelled small-molecule motor |journal=Nature |date=June 2016 |volume=534 |issue=7606 |pages=235–240 |doi=10.1038/nature18013 |pmid=27279219 |bibcode=2016Natur.534..235W |s2cid=34432774 |url=https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/397244/1/Rvsd%25207Apr2016AutonRotaryMolMotor%2520Nature.pdf }}</ref> and demonstrated a small-molecule 'robotic arm' able to transport molecular fragments between sites 2&nbsp;nm apart on a molecular platform, marking the start of so-called 'small-molecule robotics'.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kassem | first1 = S. | last2 = Lee | first2 = A. T. L.. | last3 = Leigh | first3 = D. A. | authorlink3 = David Leigh (scientist)| last4 = Markevicius | first4 = A. | last5 = Solá | first5 = J. | doi = 10.1038/nchem.2410 | pmid = 26791896 | title = Pick-up, transport and release of a molecular cargo using a small-molecule robotic arm | journal = Nature Chemistry | volume = 8 | issue = 2 | pages = 138–143 | year = 2016 | bibcode = 2016NatCh...8..138K | url = https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/pickup-transport-and-release-of-a-molecular-cargo-using-a-smallmolecule-robotic-arm(869c2832-534c-4bb4-996d-5c8c58b05ed7).html }}</ref> In 2017 the Leigh group reported the first molecular robot that can be programmed to build different molecules.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kassem | first1 = S. | last2 = Lee | first2 = A. T. L.. | last3 = Leigh | first3 = D. A. | authorlink3 = David Leigh (scientist)| last4 = Marcos | first4 = V. | last5 = Palmer | first5 = L. I. | last6 = Pisano | first6 = S. | doi = 10.1038/nature23677 | pmid = 28933436 | title = Stereodivergent synthesis with a programmable molecular machine | journal = Nature | volume = 549 | issue = 7672 | pages = 374–378 | year = 2017 | bibcode = 2017Natur.549..374K | s2cid = 205259758 | url = https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/stereodivergent-synthesis-with-a-programmable-molecular-machine(dd2b7aed-b6ff-455a-8fb7-e31851cea5e6).html }}</ref> The molecular robot could be programmed to construct any one of four different stereoisomers of a molecular product, a significant step towards a '[[molecular assembler]]'. The achievement was hailed as 'science fiction becomes fact'.<ref>{{cite tweet|number=910859158165114880|user=NatureNV|title=Science fiction becomes fact: a machine that assembles molecules<!-- full text of tweet that Twitter returned to the bot (excluding links) added by TweetCiteBot. This may be better truncated or may need expanding (TW limits responses to 140 characters) or case changes. --> |date=21 September 2017}}</ref> In 2020 the Leigh group described the 2D weaving of polymer chains,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=August |first1=David P. |last2=Dryfe |first2=Robert A. W. |last3=Haigh |first3=Sarah J. |last4=Kent |first4=Paige R. C. |last5=Leigh |first5=David A. |last6=Lemonnier |first6=Jean-François |last7=Li |first7=Zheling |last8=Muryn |first8=Christopher A. |last9=Palmer |first9=Leoni I. |last10=Song |first10=Yiwei |last11=Whitehead |first11=George F. S. |last12=Young |first12=Robert J. |title=Self-assembly of a layered two-dimensional molecularly woven fabric |journal=Nature |date=December 2020 |volume=588 |issue=7838 |pages=429–435 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-3019-9 |pmid=33328664 |bibcode=2020Natur.588..429A |s2cid=229300105 |url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/selfassembly-of-a-layered-twodimensional-molecularly-woven-fabric(beef6104-0d87-4b4b-b427-140b661c217e).html }}</ref> resulting in a molecularly-woven fabric with a [[thread count]] of 40-60 million (the finest Egyptian linen has a thread count of ~1500).

In September 2016 Leigh was suggested as one of three candidates for the potential award of a Nobel Prize for synthetic molecular machines.<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211206/rfkzZWIMgwI Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20201214074431/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rfkzZWIMgwI Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rfkzZWIMgwI| title = Who will win the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry? | via=YouTube| date = 30 September 2016 }}{{cbignore}}</ref> However, on 5 October 2016 the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] was awarded to [[J. Fraser Stoddart]], [[Ben Feringa]] and [[Jean-Pierre Sauvage]] for the design and synthesis of [[molecular machine]]s.<ref name="NP-20161005">{{cite news |author=Staff |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2016 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2016/press.html |date=5 October 2016 |work=[[Nobel Foundation]] |access-date=5 October 2016 }}</ref>

==Public engagement==
Leigh's 8<sub>19</sub> molecular knot features in the 2019 [[Guinness Book of World Records]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Guinness World Records certificate |url=http://www.catenane.net/images/general/guinness_certificate.jpg |website=catenane.net |access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref> In 2018 he commissioned 'Nanobot',<ref>{{cite web |title=Nanobot (Havana Parody) - A Capella Science ft. Dorothy Andrusiak |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ObvxPSQNMGc&feature=youtu.be  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/ObvxPSQNMGc |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|via=YouTube | date=25 August 2018 |access-date=26 May 2020}}{{cbignore}}</ref> a parody by [[Tim Blais|acapellascience]] of [[Havana (Camila Cabello song)|'Havana']] by [[Camila Cabello]], describing the science behind nanorobotics. The 'Professor David Leigh Prize for Chemistry' at [[Codsall Community High School]] encourages girls and disadvantaged children to study science at university.<ref>{{cite web |title=Leigh and the first two recipients of the 'Professor David Leigh Prize for Chemistry' at Codsall Community High School |url=https://twitter.com/ProfDaveLeigh/status/950833689826615303 |via=Twitter |access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref> Leigh is a Director and Governor of [[Withington Girls' School]].

Leigh is a former national champion [[contract bridge]] player<ref>{{cite web |title=National Pairs - Winners - Scotsman Trophy |url=https://www.sbu.org.uk/events/event-winners/92-national-pairs-winners |publisher=The Scottish Bridge Union |access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref> and an accomplished magician (ex-Edinburgh Magic Circle and the Manchester Circle of Magicians), known for blending magic and science in his public lectures.
